analysis: Orrin Augustine White (CA/IL, 1883-1969) at $500-700 -- part of the twenty-lot California consignment running through Day 1. White was a genuine California Impressionist with a real market at home, and his early work predates 1926.
problems: Wrong coast. The brief is explicit that this consignment should be identified as a block and skipped rather than analysed lot by lot -- and having now read all twenty, that judgement holds: competent West Coast painting with no Maine connection and no reason for a midcoast collection.
patience: High. California Impressionism sells best in California; buying it in Maine means selling it back into that market later.

analysis: Priscilla Jane Frazer (CA, 1907-1983) at $300-400. California consignment.
problems: Wrong coast, minor name, no criteria fit.

analysis: Paul Kratter, contemporary California, at $600-800. A living plein-air painter with an active gallery market on the West Coast.
problems: Wrong coast and a living artist selling at retail, so auction offers no discount. Part of the California block.

analysis: Will Frates (CA, 1896-1969) at $300-400 -- one of three Frates lots (1036, 1174, 1209) in the California consignment.
problems: Wrong coast. Three lots by one artist means no scarcity even within the block.

analysis: F. Michael Wood, contemporary California, at $400-600 -- one of four Wood lots (1040, 1044, 1052, 1056) plus a fifth at 1087 estimated $2,000-3,000. Five lots by one living West Coast painter is the core of this consignment.
problems: Wrong coast, living artist, five lots. Nothing here for a Maine collection.

analysis: Second F. Michael Wood at $400-600.
problems: Same as 1040.

analysis: Richard de Treville (CA/SC, 1864-1929) at $400-600. The one member of the California consignment whose dates make him genuinely antique-eligible -- he died in 1929, so most of his output predates 1926.
problems: Wrong coast still, but worth noting as the only lot in the block that touches the antique criterion. If you wanted one picture from this consignment on criteria grounds rather than taste, this would be it. Four photographs.

analysis: Third F. Michael Wood at $400-600.
problems: Same as 1040.

analysis: Donald Arvid Ealy (CA/WA, 1938-2007) at $400-600 -- one of four Ealy lots (1054, 1058, 1089, 1091).
problems: Wrong coast, four lots, no criteria fit.

analysis: Fourth F. Michael Wood at $400-600.
problems: Same as 1040.

analysis: Second Donald Ealy at $400-600.
problems: Same as 1054.

analysis: Third Donald Ealy at $600-800, with only two photographs.
problems: Same as 1054, dearer and less well documented.

analysis: Fourth Donald Ealy at $600-800.
problems: Same as 1054.

analysis: Sergio Lopez, contemporary Santa Rosa, California, at $600-800 -- one of two Lopez lots. A capable young figurative painter with a following on the West Coast.
problems: Wrong coast, living artist at gallery prices.

analysis: Second Sergio Lopez at $600-800.
problems: Same as 1093.

analysis: Gerald F. Brommer (CA, 1927-2020) at $500-700. Brommer was a widely published watercolour instructor with a large following among amateur painters, which supports a steady but modest market.
problems: Wrong coast. Note this lot sits in the middle of the old 1142-1161 gap the hand-off flagged -- now closed.

analysis: Second Will Frates at $700-900.
problems: Wrong coast, three Frates lots in the sale.

analysis: Third Will Frates at $1,000-1,500 -- the most expensive Frates and out of band.
problems: Out of band and wrong coast.

analysis: Michele Usibelli, contemporary California, at $250-350 -- the cheapest lot in the California block.
problems: Wrong coast, living artist.

analysis: Tony Bell (CA/TX, 1950-199-) at $300-400. Note the catalogue gives his death year as '199' -- a truncated entry, another small cataloguing failure.
problems: Wrong coast and the dates are incomplete in the entry itself.

analysis: Marguerite Kirmse (CT/UK, 1885-1954) at $800-1,200. Kirmse was the great dog etcher of the interwar period -- terriers especially -- and dog-print collectors are a real and durable market. Her working life straddles the antique line.
problems: Only just inside the band. Establish whether this is an original etching (usually pencil-signed) or a later photographic reproduction, which are common. Four photographs.
patience: Moderate. Kirmse etchings appear regularly and are well documented.

analysis: Shmuel Tepler (Israel/Poland, 1918-1998) at $300-400. One of several Israeli painters scattered through Day 1 (1050, 1225, 1366, 1448), suggesting a small related consignment.
problems: No criteria fit -- not antique, not Maine, no metal. Israeli mid-century painting has a specialist market concentrated in Israel and New York.

analysis: Zoltan Sepeshy (1898-1974) at $800-1,200. Sepeshy was a genuinely significant figure -- director of Cranbrook Academy and a serious American modernist with museum holdings. Note the catalogue misspells Hungary as 'HUNGSRY'.
problems: Only just inside the band, no Maine or antique claim. His market is respectable but not deep. Four photographs.

analysis: August Mosca (NY/Italy, 1907-2003) at $300-400. A minor New York modernist.
problems: No criteria fit. Thin market record.

analysis: Arthur Beaumont (1877-1956) at $300-400. If this is the Arthur Beaumont who was the US Navy's official war artist, his marine watercolours have a genuine following -- and at $300 that would be good value.
problems: The catalogue gives only 'NY' and dates that do not quite match the Navy painter (1890-1978), so this may be a different Arthur Beaumont. Establish which before assuming the market. Four photographs.

analysis: Julius Wolfgang Schulein (NY/Germany, 1881-1970) at $400-600. A German emigre Expressionist with a modest market.
problems: No criteria fit.

analysis: Yitzhak Frenkel-Frenel (Israel/Ukraine, 1899-1981) at $400-600, with a second at 2376. Frenkel is a significant name in Israeli art history.
problems: No criteria fit for this brief, and his market is concentrated in Israel. Five photographs.

analysis: Cecil Vezin Grant (NJ, 1880-1973) at $400-600.
problems: Minor name, no criteria fit. Note the catalogue punctuates the state as 'NJ.' with a stray period.

analysis: Margaret Fitzhugh Browne (MA, 1884-1972) at $400-600. A Boston-trained portrait and still-life painter, and part of the generation of New England women painters whose work has been reassessed upward.
problems: Long career straddling the antique line, so an early work could qualify -- but nothing here dates it. Four photographs.

analysis: Mary Brewster Hazelton (1868-1953) at $600-800. Hazelton was a serious Boston School painter -- the first woman to win the Hallgarten Prize -- and exactly the sort of turn-of-the-century American woman artist whose market has been rising as the reassessment continues. A substantial part of her output predates 1926.
problems: Border on age until the picture is dated. Boston School portraits are a soft market despite the reassessment. Four photographs -- check for relining and for overcleaning in the flesh tones.
patience: Moderate. Hazelton appears periodically and is consistently underpriced relative to her contemporaries.

analysis: Iris Andrews Miller (Detroit, 1881-1981) at $500-800 -- one of three Miller lots (1081, 1152, 1154). A hundred-year life and three lots in one sale.
problems: No criteria fit, minor name, and only two photographs here. Three lots means no scarcity.

analysis: Second Iris Andrews Miller at $800-1,000.
problems: Same as 1081, dearer.

analysis: The description dates it: 'Sef Portrait' [sic], oil on canvas, CIRCA 1925, signed lower right, note on stretcher indicates the title was on the now missing frame. That puts it on the antique line rather than in the mid-century where I had it, and a dated self-portrait by a woman painter working in Detroit in 1925 is a more interesting object than an undated one. Iris Andrews Miller (1881-1981) still has essentially no auction record, so the age is the only thing that has changed.
problems: 'Loss to bottom edge' is stated and on an oil on canvas that means paint loss, not just frame wear. The original frame is gone and with it the title. No auction record for the artist. c.1925 straddles the antique line, hence border. The catalogue misspells 'Self' in the title, which tells you how carefully this was catalogued.

analysis: Borje Skohg (Sweden, 1923-2006) at $300-400.
problems: No criteria fit and a Scandinavian market that does not travel. Two photographs.

analysis: Jerome Howes (NY/MA, 1955- ) at $800-1,200. A living contemporary painter.
problems: Only just inside the band, no criteria fit.

analysis: Zuzana Chalupova (Serbia, 1925-2001) at $600-800 with six photographs. Chalupova was a well-known Serbian naive painter of the Kovacica school, and naive art has its own international collecting base.
problems: No criteria fit for this brief. The naive-art market is concentrated in Europe.

analysis: Paul Starrett Sample (NY/CA/VT, 1896-1974) at $600-800. Sample was a significant American Regionalist -- artist-in-residence at Dartmouth, and his New England winter scenes are properly collected.
problems: At $600-800 this will be a watercolour or a print rather than one of the oils that make five figures. Establish which. Five photographs. Vermont rather than Maine, but the same northern New England idiom.
patience: Moderate. Sample's works on paper are the affordable end of a good name.

analysis: Wayne Beam Morrell (MA/NJ, 1923-2013) at $800-1,200. A Rockport, Massachusetts painter whose harbour and winter scenes sell steadily.
problems: Only just inside the band. Morrell was extremely prolific -- supply is deep and prices have been flat. Five photographs.

analysis: Charles Stepule (CT/MA, 1911-2006) at $800-1,200. A competent New England painter with a modest market.
problems: Only just inside the band, no Maine or antique claim.

analysis: Andre Gisson (1921-2003) at $700-900. Gisson -- real name Anders Gittelson -- painted large numbers of pleasant Impressionist-style pictures that sell readily and appreciate very little.
problems: Extremely prolific, so supply is effectively unlimited and the market is flat. The catalogue's parenthetical '(GITTELON)' acknowledges the pseudonym. No criteria fit.

analysis: Nan Greacen, also known as Favre (1909-1999), at $600-900. Daughter of the Impressionist Edmund Greacen.
problems: No criteria fit. Her market is much smaller than her father's, and the alias fragments the comparable record.

analysis: William Meyerowitz (1887-1981) at $1,000-1,500. A Gloucester painter and etcher of real standing whose Cape Ann subjects are collected in New England. Note the catalogue gives his state as CA, which is wrong -- he was a Massachusetts and New York artist.
problems: Out of band. At this estimate it may be an oil rather than an etching; his etchings are $200-400 and would be in band, so establish the medium. Another state-attribution error.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, but his etchings are worth watching for at other sales.

analysis: Charles Warde Traver (NY/NJ, 1870-1945) at $1,000-2,000. Working life straddles the antique line.
problems: Out of band. Minor name with a thin record, so the wide estimate spread is the house guessing.

analysis: J. Winthrop Andrews (MA/NY/Bermuda, 1879-1964) at $600-800 with five photographs. Long career straddling the antique line.
problems: Minor name. The Bermuda association suggests tropical subjects, which have less appeal in a Maine collection than a New England scene would.

analysis: William Henry Holmes (1846-1933) at $400-600. Holmes is a genuinely interesting figure -- a geological survey artist who illustrated the Grand Canyon and later directed the National Gallery -- and the great bulk of his output long predates 1926. A named maker with real historical standing at a low price.
problems: Border on age only because he lived to 1933; in practice most of his work is 19th century. Four photographs. His topographical watercolours are the desirable work; establish the medium and subject.
patience: Moderate. Holmes appears rarely and is undervalued relative to his historical importance.

analysis: Lambro Ahlas (1927-2021), portrait of a ballet dancer, at $400-600.
problems: No criteria fit and a thin market record. Portraits of anonymous sitters are also the hardest pictures to resell.

analysis: Tim Gaydos (NJ, 1941- ) at $800-1,000. A realist painter of urban subjects with a modest following.
problems: No criteria fit, living artist, top of the band.

analysis: Perry Winkler, contemporary Pennsylvania, at $600-800.
problems: No criteria fit, living artist.

analysis: Antonio Ruiz (Mexico, 1897-1964) at $500-700. Ruiz was a significant Mexican modernist -- a contemporary of Rivera and Kahlo -- so if genuine this would be substantially underpriced.
problems: That is the warning, not the opportunity: a genuine Ruiz would not be $500. Treat a suspiciously cheap significant name as a red flag first. Establish medium and provenance, and consider whether this is a different Antonio Ruiz. Four photographs.

analysis: William J. Maloney (MA/Italy, 1932-2023) at $250-350, with a second at 3403 estimated $1,000-1,500.
problems: No criteria fit. Only two photographs. The eight-fold estimate gap between the two Maloney lots suggests this is a minor work.

analysis: Louis (Luigi) Bosa (NY/PA/Italy, 1905-1991) at $200-300 -- one of the cheapest paintings in Day 1.
problems: No criteria fit. Bosa's market is modest and his output large.

analysis: Elizabeth E. Case (NY, 1858-1951) at $600-800. A long career beginning well before 1926, so an early work would qualify on age, and another of the period women painters worth watching.
problems: Very thin market record. Three photographs. Look for a date.

analysis: James De Martin (NY, 1923-2003) at $400-600 with five photographs.
problems: No criteria fit, minor name.

analysis: Judy Prisoc, contemporary Gig Harbor, Washington, at $250-350 with a marine subject.
problems: Wrong coast, living artist, two photographs. The marine subject is the only thing connecting it to the brief and that is not enough.

analysis: Axel Olson Haldrup (Denmark, 1890-1977) at $600-800 with four photographs.
problems: No criteria fit and a Danish market that does not travel to Maine.

analysis: Mark Osman Curtis, also known as Th. Friis (Norway/Scotland, 1879-1959), at $600-800. Working life straddles the antique line and Scandinavian-Scottish marine painting is competent stuff.
problems: An artist working under two names, which fragments the comparable record and usually signals commercial production under a pseudonym. No Maine link. Four photographs.

analysis: John A. Ruthven (NY, 1924- ) at $300-500 -- the first of five consecutive Ruthven lots (1317-1321). Ruthven was a well-known wildlife artist in the Audubon tradition whose prints were published in very large editions.
problems: Five lots in a row of a widely published print-maker is the definition of no scarcity. Ruthven's signed limited editions were often 1,000-plus impressions, and the secondary market for them is weak. Establish whether these are prints or originals, but expect prints.
patience: Very high -- five in this sale and thousands in circulation.

analysis: Second Ruthven at $300-500.
problems: Same as 1317.

analysis: Third Ruthven at $600-800 -- the dearest of the five.
problems: Same as 1317, and no stated reason for the higher estimate.

analysis: Fourth Ruthven at $300-500.
problems: Same as 1317.

analysis: Fifth and last Ruthven at $300-500.
problems: Same as 1317.

analysis: Orson Byron Lowell (NY, 1871-1956) at $350-550. Lowell was a prolific magazine illustrator for Life and Judge, and original illustration art of that era has a dedicated following. Much of his output predates 1926.
problems: Illustration art is bought for the image and the publication, so establish whether this was published and where. Four photographs.

analysis: Dmitry Borisovitch Lion (Russia, 1925-1993) at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band, no criteria fit, and a Soviet-era market concentrated abroad. Three photographs.

analysis: Susan Blackwood (MT/CO/IL, 1948- ) at $300-400.
problems: No criteria fit, living artist. Note the catalogue punctuates 'IL.' with a stray period.

analysis: Harold Wolpoff (MA, 1924-2013) at $300-500 with five photographs.
problems: No criteria fit, minor name.

analysis: Thompson Lehnert (PA/OH, 1931-2020) at $300-400 with five photographs.
problems: No criteria fit.

analysis: Jack Gerber (PA, 1927-2021) at $250-350.
problems: No criteria fit.

analysis: Sally Jessy Raphael (NY, 1938- ) at $400-600 -- the television talk-show host, painting as an avocation. Celebrity association rather than artistic standing.
problems: Celebrity art is a category unto itself: the value depends entirely on the celebrity's currency, which is a depreciating asset. No criteria fit at all.

analysis: Bruce Backman Turner (MA, 1941- ) at $300-400. A Rockport, Massachusetts painter.
problems: Living artist, no criteria fit.

analysis: Gilbert Haven Smith (VT/IL, 1882-1959) at $500-700. A Vermont painter whose career begins well before 1926.
problems: Minor name, thin record, no Maine link. Four photographs.

analysis: Four small paintings by James Mickelson (MA, 1926-1998) at $500-700, with a fifth single work at 1410 for the same money. Four pictures in one lot is the better value of the two.
problems: Minor name. Six photographs for four works. Buying four means four things to hang or store; establish sizes.
patience: High -- two Mickelson lots in the sale.

analysis: A single James Mickelson at $500-700 -- the same estimate as the four-picture lot at 1406.
problems: Paying the same for one as for four makes no sense unless this is substantially better. Compare them at preview; otherwise bid 1406.

analysis: Jorge Wilmot (Mexican, 1928-2012), 'Bird on Rock', at $200-300, with a companion at 1422. Wilmot is better known as a ceramicist -- he revived Tonala pottery -- than as a painter.
problems: No criteria fit. His reputation rests on ceramics, so paintings are peripheral to his market.

analysis: Second Jorge Wilmot, 'Bird Among Blossoms', at $200-300.
problems: Same as 1420.

analysis: A.D. Greer (NY/TX/OK, 1904-1998) at $500-700. Greer painted large numbers of competent traditional landscapes.
problems: Very prolific, so supply is deep and prices flat. No criteria fit.

analysis: Louis Maria Niels Peder Moe (Norway, 1857-1945) at $300-400. A long career beginning in the 1880s, so most of the output predates 1926.
problems: Norwegian market, no Maine link. Four photographs.

analysis: Lothar Burger (Austria, 1866-1943) at $300-500 with five photographs. Career beginning in the 1890s, so largely antique-eligible.
problems: Austrian market, no criteria fit beyond possible age and a name. Establish a date on the work.

analysis: Theo Tobiasse (NY/France/Israel, 1927-2012) at $400-500. Tobiasse has a real market in France and Israel and produced a great deal of graphic work.
problems: At this price it is a print rather than a painting. No criteria fit. Five photographs.

analysis: An Edwin A. Harvey watercolour at $200-300 with six photographs -- unusually good disclosure for a cheap lot.
problems: No dates for the artist, so effectively an unidentified signature with no period. Cheap enough that the six photographs let you judge it on the image alone.

analysis: Frederick Kubitz, contemporary Massachusetts, at $200-300.
problems: Living artist, no criteria fit.

analysis: Catalogued as 'WALT FRANCIS (WALTER) KUHN (NY/CA, 1877-1949)' at $400-500. Walt Kuhn is a major American modernist -- an Armory Show organiser whose clown and showgirl paintings are in every major museum -- so a genuine Kuhn at $400 would be extraordinary.
problems: Which is exactly why it needs checking rather than believing. The catalogue's mangled name form and the CA attribution do not inspire confidence, and a real Kuhn oil is a five-figure object. Either this is a minor work on paper, a misattribution, or a different artist. Treat a suspiciously cheap major name as a red flag first, then investigate.
patience: Moderate -- worth twenty minutes at preview precisely because the upside if right is large.

analysis: Edouard Febvre (France, 1885-1967) at $300-400 with four photographs.
problems: No criteria fit, minor French name.

analysis: Massimo Campigli (1895-1971) at $300-400. Campigli is a significant Italian modernist, so at this price it is a print.
problems: Only two photographs and no medium stated. Campigli's lithographs are common; his paintings are not remotely in this range. Establish edition and signature.

analysis: Frank Gervasi (NY, 1895-1986) at $500-700 with five photographs.
problems: No criteria fit, minor name.

analysis: Raoul Verin (France, 1865-1943) at $300-400 with six photographs -- the last painting lot of Day 1. Career beginning in the 1890s so largely antique-eligible.
problems: Minor French name with no Maine or American connection. Six photographs is good disclosure for the price.

analysis: Dated by the description, and it clears the antique line: '(2 vols): "The History of Portrait Miniatures" by George C. Williamson, Litt.D. London, George Bell and Sons, 1904, printed by Chiswick Press, white buckram binding with gilt decoration, deckled edge pages'. Williamson's is the standard reference on the subject and the 1904 Bell edition on deckled paper from the Chiswick Press is the good one. Genuinely antique, and directly useful given how many miniatures are in this sale -- though note that most of those turn out to be painted on ivory and therefore unbuyable.
problems: White buckram is the worst possible binding for survival: it soils, foxes and browns, and it cannot be cleaned. Check the plates are all present, since illustrated reference books of this date are routinely broken for them. Reference books have a shallow resale market whatever their age.

analysis: A pair of Chinese export paintings on pith paper, 19th century, at $200-300. Catalogued to the century so genuinely antique, and cheap. Pith paper works were made in Canton for the export trade and are attractive small decorative objects.
problems: Pith paper is extremely fragile -- it cracks, flakes and loses pigment, and losses cannot be repaired. Check both sheets carefully. Three of these lots appear in the sale (1403, 1409, plus 2485 and 2506 in Day 2), so no scarcity.

analysis: A large Chinese pith painting, 19th century, at $300-400. Larger than 1403 and catalogued to the century.
problems: Same fragility. Large pith sheets are more prone to cracking than small ones because there is more area to flex.

analysis: A late Qing scroll painting of a noblewoman at $200-300. Late Qing means roughly 1875-1911, so antique-eligible on the catalogue's own dating.
problems: Part of the substantial Chinese decorative group running through Day 1, a category where reproduction is endemic and unverifiable from photographs. Scroll paintings of court ladies were produced in enormous quantity for export and continue to be. Four photographs.
